deep-dive.title: Lifting Conversion 6% by Sweating the Small Stuff

context.stakes: Application completion on our largest brand had slid 8% over two quarters, and nobody could point to a release that caused it.

problem.summary: Completion rates were falling slowly, with no single cause we could see in our dashboards.

details.detail: A few sharp drops, plus a slow leak in between
No deployment lined up with the losses
Page-level analytics showed where people left, not why

phase.name: Discovery
phase.step: Watched hundreds of session replays from abandoned applications
Added detailed client-side logging with engineering to see errors users never reported
Reviewed every change shipped in the prior six months

phase.name: Hypothesis
phase.step: Narrowed it to three suspects: bank account linking, a new vendor card form, and phone verification
Ranked them by how many applicants each touched and how hard each was to fix

phase.name: Execution
phase.step: Found the vendor card form, embedded in an iFrame, silently failing on older phones, and added a fallback path
Fixed dozens of smaller issues the new logging surfaced
Kept a weekly replay review going after the numbers recovered

deep-dive.title: Cutting Third-Party Fraud 85% Without Losing Applicants

context.stakes: Fraud rings using stolen identities were costing us millions a year, and every fraud tool we'd tried before had hurt conversion.

problem.summary: Stolen personal data made fraudulent applications look identical to real ones, and instant decisions gave us seconds to tell them apart.

details.detail: Fraud losses well above our risk tolerance
Stolen data meant identity checks on name and SSN alone were useless
Decisions still had to be instant and fair-lending compliant

phase.name: Collaboration
phase.step: Risk brought us a document and selfie verification vendor
We pulled device data (80% of applicants were on phones) and brought compliance in early

phase.name: Design and Build
phase.step: Placed verification only where the risk model flagged an application
Built a hand-off so desktop applicants could finish the check on their phone
Added an escape path so real customers were never stuck

phase.name: Rollout
phase.step: Tested copy and step order to raise completion of the check
Tracked fraud and conversion side by side every week

metric.label: Completion rate for the new check

deep-dive.title: Lowering Write-offs 1.5% by Giving Borrowers a Payoff Date

context.stakes: Our new line of credit was growing fast, but customers kept calling to ask the same question: when will this be paid off?

problem.summary: Minimum payments on a revolving line gave customers no end date, and the uncertainty was showing up in support calls and late payments.

details.detail: Customers couldn't tell when they'd be debt-free
Card issuers were already offering fixed payment plans
Finance worried faster payoff would shrink the portfolio

phase.name: Research
phase.step: Tagged a quarter of support calls to size the payoff question
Reviewed how card issuers presented fixed payment plans

phase.name: Modeling
phase.step: Rebuilt the line of credit math in a spreadsheet, accurate to the penny
Simulated each customer's balance forward under several payment plans
Found a large share of customers headed for delinquency, and that a fixed payment kept many of them current

phase.name: Build and Launch
phase.step: Designed a payment choice screen that showed the payoff date and total interest saved
Handed engineering the spreadsheet as the test oracle for the new calculation
Piloted in two states before rolling out everywhere

metric.label: Of customers chose a fixed plan
"When will I be paid off?" calls

deep-dive.title: Building Connected Equipment Before It Had a Name

context.stakes: Operators found out about engine problems when the engine shut down. On a remote pump station, that meant a day of lost output and a long drive.

problem.summary: Our displays showed a warning lamp and a few gauges. Operators needed to see trouble coming.

details.detail: Small screens with almost no diagnostic data
No way to check on equipment without driving out to it
Web technology was unproven on rugged embedded hardware

phase.name: Field Research
phase.step: Installed prototypes on working sites and watched operators use them
Rode along with service technicians on breakdown calls

phase.name: Bigger Screens
phase.step: Designed larger displays with trends so operators could spot drift early
Made every control usable with gloves and in direct sun

phase.name: Embedded Web
phase.step: Ran a web server on the display so the same screens worked remotely
Bridged engine data onto plant networks with standard industrial protocols

metric.label: Web-based display in the product line

image.alt: Placeholder for a large engine display
image.caption: Larger displays put trends in front of operators for the first time

deep-dive.title: Moving 400K Customers to a New Login Without Anyone Noticing

context.stakes: Our homegrown login system was our top support driver and a security liability, but customers needed uninterrupted access to their accounts.

problem.summary: The old login couldn't support modern multi-factor options, and every outage hit every brand at once.

details.detail: Sign-in trouble was the number one reason customers called
Text-message codes failed often with some carriers

phase.name: Planning
phase.step: Mapped every place a customer signs in or resets a password
Designed a parallel run so either system could serve any customer

phase.name: Migration
phase.step: Moved employee accounts first, then the smallest brand
Migrated customers silently at their next successful sign-in

deep-dive.title: Kestrel Credit: Launching a $25M Lending Brand

context.stakes: Our flagship brand had saturated its market. Growth had to come from customers we weren't reaching yet.

problem.summary: Borrowers with fair credit were stuck between banks that turned them down and lenders that overcharged them.

details.detail: A real gap between prime lenders and high-cost options
No brand recognition in that segment

phase.name: Discovery
phase.step: Interviewed borrowers about what they disliked in their last loan
Positioned the brand around progress, not just approval

phase.name: Build
phase.step: Reused the shared platform to cut time to market
Shortened the application for a credit tier that expects less paperwork

phase.name: Launch
phase.step: Rolled out state by state, simplest regulation first
Tuned underwriting on early repayment data

metric.label: Don't launch invite-only. It added little and became tech debt the day we opened up.

deep-dive.title: Lumen: Turning an Installment Loan into a Line of Credit

context.stakes: Our installment loan was flat. A line of credit could lower payments and let customers borrow again without reapplying.

problem.summary: Customers had to reapply every time they needed more money, and the payments were higher than they needed to be.

details.detail: Repeat customers went through a full application each time
A line of credit would lower the typical payment

phase.name: Product
phase.step: Extended the loan system to support revolving balances
Built a conversion journey for existing installment customers

phase.name: Servicing
phase.step: Redesigned the account dashboard around available credit
Added a fixed payment option after customers asked for an end date

metric.label: Portfolio growth in the first year
Typical monthly payment than the old loan

image.caption: Account dashboard built around available credit

deep-dive.title: Helm Display: A Glass Cockpit for Recreational Boats

context.stakes: Boat builders wanted the glass-cockpit look of modern aircraft. Our display was a decade old.

problem.summary: The old display showed a few numbers and a warning lamp, and it couldn't keep up with new engine features.

details.detail: No support for newer multi-engine controls
Alarms were a light with no explanation

phase.name: Discovery
phase.step: Spent days aboard boats with captains and builders

phase.name: Design
phase.step: Built configurable multi-engine views that scaled across screen sizes
Added night and day modes for the bridge
Replaced alarm lamps with plain-language messages

image.alt: Placeholder for a marine helm display
image.caption: Multi-engine helm view with day and night modes

deep-dive.title: Pump Station Controller: Simple Controls for Remote Sites

context.stakes: Farm and municipal customers ran single engines on remote pumps, with a tight budget for controls.

problem.summary: The available controls were either too basic to diagnose anything or too expensive for a single pump.

details.detail: Three gauges and a start button, with no fault information
Every fault meant a technician visit

phase.name: Simplify
phase.step: Stripped a multi-engine platform down to what one pump needs
Moved control logic into the display to lower hardware cost

phase.name: Ship
phase.step: Wrote plain-English fault messages in place of blink codes
Kept the embedded web server so sites could be checked remotely

metric.label: To diagnose a fault, down from hours
